title: Anti-joins: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS
objective: Find rows that have NO match in another table using LEFT JOIN … IS NULL and NOT EXISTS, and avoid the NOT IN + NULL trap.
context: Some of the most valuable questions are about absence: customers who never ordered, products that never sold, suppliers we pay for but don't stock, references to records that don't exist. These are anti-joins: keep the left rows that have no partner on the right.

exercises.title: Customers who never ordered
exercises.question: Marketing wants a win-back list: customers who have never placed any order.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name and signup_date for customers with no row in orders (any status). Use LEFT JOIN … IS NULL.
hints: LEFT JOIN keeps every customer; customers without orders get NULL order columns.
Test a right-side column that can never be NULL for a real match — the key.
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
exercises.why: Activation and win-back campaigns start from 'who did nothing'. The anti-join is the only way to see rows that by definition left no trace in the activity table.

recall.q: Why test o.order_id IS NULL rather than any orders column?
recall.a: order_id is the key, never NULL in a real match — a nullable column could be NULL in matched rows too.

exercises.join_notes: The LEFT JOIN returns 62 rows: 59 order rows for 17 customers (customer 1 alone repeats 9 times) plus 3 NULL-extended rows for customers 18 (Mia Lewis), 19 (alice johnson) and 20 (Zoe Turner). WHERE o.order_id IS NULL keeps exactly those 3. Orphan order 31 (customer 99) is irrelevant here — it's unmatched on the RIGHT side, which a LEFT JOIN discards.

exercises.title: Products never sold
exercises.question: Merchandising wants to delist dead stock: which products have never appeared on any order line?
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and category for products with no row in order_items. Use NOT EXISTS.
hints: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE <correlation>) keeps rows with no match.
Correlate the subquery to the outer product: i.product_id = p.product_id.
SELECT ... FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i WHERE i.product_id = p.product_id);
exercises.why: NOT EXISTS reads like the business question ('there is no sale for this product'), never multiplies rows, and is immune to the NULL trap.

recall.q: Does it matter what NOT EXISTS's subquery SELECTs?
recall.a: No — only whether any row exists. SELECT 1 is the convention.

exercises.join_notes: NOT EXISTS never multiplies: each of the 25 products is tested once, however many of the 150 lines mention it. 22 products have at least one line; 23 (Smart Watch), 24 (Linen Tablecloth) and 25 (Tennis Racket) have none → 3 rows. The LEFT JOIN version would first build 153 rows (150 lines + 3 NULL rows) before filtering.

exercises.title: Suppliers with no products
exercises.question: Procurement wants to close supplier accounts that supply nothing in our catalog.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id, supplier_name and country for suppliers that no product references via products.supplier_id.
hints: Left table = suppliers, evidence table = products.
Tempted by NOT IN (SELECT supplier_id FROM products)? Run it and count the rows first.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id)
exercises.why: This is the textbook case where NOT IN silently fails: one NULL foreign key in the subquery and the 'unused suppliers' report comes back empty — looking like good news.

recall.q: What does `5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` evaluate to?
recall.a: NULL (unknown), not TRUE — so the row is filtered out. One NULL poisons NOT IN.

exercises.join_notes: Suppliers 1-4 are referenced by 23 products; supplier 5 (Andes Trading, NULL country) by none → 1 row, with country NULL (a NULL attribute, not a failed match). `WHERE supplier_id NOT IN (SELECT supplier_id FROM products)` returns 0 rows because product 22's supplier_id is NULL; product 21's supplier_id 9 points to no supplier, which doesn't affect this direction at all.

exercises.title: Broken supplier references
exercises.question: Data quality wants products whose supplier_id is filled in but points at a supplier that doesn't exist.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id, product_name and supplier_id for products whose supplier_id is NOT NULL and has no matching row in suppliers. Products with a NULL supplier_id are a different issue and must be excluded.
hints: Anti-join products → suppliers.
A NULL supplier_id also finds no supplier — exclude it explicitly.
LEFT JOIN suppliers s ON s.supplier_id = p.supplier_id WHERE s.supplier_id IS NULL AND p.supplier_id IS NOT NULL
exercises.why: Orphaned foreign keys ('points to nothing') and missing foreign keys ('points nowhere') have different root causes and owners; a good data-quality check separates them.

recall.q: Why does a product with a NULL supplier_id show up in a LEFT JOIN … IS NULL anti-join?
recall.a: NULL never equals anything, so it finds no supplier and gets NULL right-side columns like a true orphan.

exercises.join_notes: supplier_id is unique in suppliers, so the LEFT JOIN keeps exactly 25 rows. 23 products match; 2 get NULL supplier columns: product 21 (Water Bottle, supplier_id 9 — no such supplier) and product 22 (Phone Stand, supplier_id NULL). The extra p.supplier_id IS NOT NULL removes 22, leaving 1 true orphan reference.

exercises.title: Customers with no valid order
exercises.question: Finance asks: which customers have never generated revenue — no completed, shipped or returned order (cancelled/pending ones don't count)?
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id and name for customers with no valid order (valid = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')). Customers with only cancelled/pending orders, or no orders at all, qualify.
hints: The status filter describes which orders count as a match — so it belongs with the match condition, not in the final WHERE.
LEFT JOIN orders ON customer_id AND status IN (...), then WHERE o.order_id IS NULL. (Or NOT EXISTS with the status in the subquery.)
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
exercises.why: Filtered anti-joins ('no purchase in the last 90 days', 'no valid order') are everyday churn logic, and putting the filter in WHERE is the most common way they break.

recall.q: In a LEFT JOIN anti-join, where must conditions on the right table go?
recall.a: In the ON clause (or inside NOT EXISTS). In WHERE they reject the NULL rows you're looking for.

exercises.join_notes: With the status filter in ON, only valid orders can match: 16 customers match one or more valid orders, 4 get NULLs — 16 (Ava Thompson, whose only order 48 is cancelled), 18, 19 and 20 (no orders). Result 4 rows. If you move the status test to WHERE, the NULL rows fail `o.order_status IN (...)` and the result is 0 rows; if you drop it, customer 16 disappears because her cancelled order counts as a match.

exercises.title: The NOT IN trap: unused category names
exercises.question: The catalog team wants category names from the category tree that no product is tagged with. Their NOT IN query says 'none' — is that true?
exercises.prompt: Return category_id and category_name for categories whose category_name does not equal any products.category. (products.category contains a NULL for product 20 — your query must still return the right answer.)
hints: Try `WHERE category_name NOT IN (SELECT category FROM products)` and count the rows. Why?
Use NOT EXISTS, or add WHERE category IS NOT NULL inside the NOT IN subquery.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.category = c.category_name)
exercises.why: NOT IN against a nullable column is a silent-failure bug: no error, just an empty result that looks like 'all good'. Default to NOT EXISTS.

recall.q: Name two ways to make a NOT IN anti-join NULL-safe.
recall.a: Use NOT EXISTS instead, or filter the subquery with WHERE col IS NOT NULL.

exercises.join_notes: The join key here is a text label (category_name = category), not an id. Only 5 of 14 category names (Electronics, Home, Apparel, Books, Sports) are used by products; the other 9 — All Products, Audio, Computer Accessories, Kitchen, Decor, Footwear, Outerwear, Fitness, Strength Training — are returned. The NOT IN version returns 0 rows because product 20's NULL category makes every `name <> NULL` test unknown.

exercises.title: Products never sold to the North region
exercises.question: The North regional manager wants to know which catalog products have never been bought by a North customer in a valid order.
exercises.prompt: Return product_id and product_name for products with no order line in a valid order (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) placed by a customer whose region is 'North'. Products never sold at all also qualify.
hints: The 'evidence' is itself a join: order_items → orders → customers.
Put that whole join, plus the region and status filters, inside NOT EXISTS and correlate on product_id.
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON ... JOIN customers c ON ... WHERE i.product_id = p.product_id AND c.region = 'North' AND o.order_status IN (...))
exercises.why: Real 'never' questions are scoped (never in this region / channel / period). NOT EXISTS with an inner join inside scales to any amount of scoping without fan-out.

recall.q: Why is NOT EXISTS convenient when the 'evidence' needs several joined tables?
recall.a: The subquery can contain any joins and filters; the outer query stays one row per product, so nothing multiplies.

exercises.join_notes: Inside the subquery the lines are joined to orders and customers and filtered to North + valid; 14 products have at least one such line, 11 don't: 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20 plus never-sold 23, 24, 25. Order 31 (customer 99) can never count as North — its customer doesn't exist, so the inner join inside drops it. With a LEFT JOIN approach the region/status filters must all live in the ON clauses, which is far easier to get wrong.

worked_example.question: Which orders reference a customer that doesn't exist (orphan orders)?
worked_example.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.order_status
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
worked_example.explanation: All 60 orders survive the LEFT JOIN; 59 find their customer and only order 31 (customer_id 99) gets NULLs on the customer side. Testing the right table's key for NULL keeps exactly the unmatched row.

recipe:
**Recipe: anti-join in 4 moves**

1. Left table = the things you want to list (customers). Right table = the evidence of activity (orders).
2. **Pattern A — LEFT JOIN … IS NULL:** left join, then keep rows where a *never-NULL* right column
   (its key) is NULL.
3. **Pattern B — NOT EXISTS:** keep left rows for which a correlated subquery finds nothing.
4. Put **conditions about the right side** (status, region, date) *inside* the ON clause or the
   subquery — never in the outer WHERE, or you turn the anti-join back into an inner join.

```sql
-- A: LEFT JOIN anti-join
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

-- B: NOT EXISTS (usually the clearest and safest)
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
```

**The NOT IN trap:** `x NOT IN (SELECT col ...)` returns **no rows at all** if `col` contains a single
NULL, because `x <> NULL` is unknown. Products has a NULL `supplier_id` (product 22) and a NULL
`category` (product 20), so `NOT IN (SELECT supplier_id FROM products)` silently returns nothing.
Use NOT EXISTS, or add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery.

**Snowflake:** same SQL. Snowflake's optimizer turns NOT EXISTS into an anti-join internally; you
may see "ANTI JOIN" in the query profile.
common_mistakes: Testing a nullable right-side column for IS NULL instead of the right table's key.
Putting right-table filters (status, region, date) in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN — the anti-join returns nothing.
Using NOT IN against a column that can be NULL — the whole result silently becomes empty.
Forgetting that a NULL foreign key also looks 'unmatched' in a LEFT JOIN anti-join.
Confusing directions: orphan orders (unmatched on the orders side) vs customers without orders (unmatched on the customers side).
recall: Write the two standard anti-join patterns.
LEFT JOIN r ON … WHERE r.key IS NULL; and WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM r WHERE r.key = l.key).
Why can NOT IN return zero rows unexpectedly?
If the subquery returns any NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never TRUE.
NOT EXISTS never does; LEFT JOIN … IS NULL can't in its output either, because only unmatched (single NULL-extended) rows survive.
